newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH ALLOTMENT HOLDER GROUP RETAINS URBAN LAND.
newsitem.headline: POLISH ALLOTMENT HOLDER GROUP RETAINS URBAN LAND.

text.p: Poland's parliament overruled a court ruling on Friday and upheld a new law handing huge tracts of valuable urban real estate to an association of allotment garden holders, despite anguished protests from city councils.

The legal amendment, first passed in 1995 with the support of the ruling left-wing coalition, gives hosts of the small, lovingly-tended gardens rented by almost a million Poles to the Polish Association of Allotment Holders on a 99-year-lease.
The ruling affects 44,000 hectares of land around Poland much of which is on prime urban building land, estimated to be worth between $1 billion and $2 billion in Warsaw alone.

City councils said that while they wished to preserve the gardens where possible, some of this land was essential for development such as vitally-needed housing or roads and they were being stripped of their ownership rights.
In November the country's Constitutional Tribunal upheld the council's objections and also rejected the decision to grant control to only one association of allotment holders.

But a two-thirds parliamentary majority can overthrow the rulings of the tribunal, which exists to ensure new laws conform with the constitution. Deputies did so on Friday by 267 votes to 74 with eight abstentions, PAP news agency reported.
The ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and its Peasant party allies who backed the law, said they were safeguarding plot holders who now rent from municipalities.

This stance is popular among millions of voters for whom such gardens with their little summer houses offer a weekend family escape from cramped apartments -- or help in fleshing out a meagre income by growing food or flowers for sale.
Poland faces parliamentary elections this year and some chiefs of the allotment holders' association have promised to back the SLD in return for its support.

Warsaw city President Marcin Swiecicki told Reuters last year that in Warsaw's central district alone the issue concerned about 400 hectares of land, at a time when prime sites were commanding up to $1,000 a square metre.

The mayor, a member of the centrist Union for Freedom (UW) which opposed the new law, said that even if the land value was assessed far lower: "Four hundred hectares reaches a value of more than $1 billion, in the city centre." -- Anthony Barker +48 22 653 9700
